# Bass v. TTUHSC — Honesty Check on Court Filings (Plain-Language Summary)

This is a plain-language guide to a set of honesty problems found in court filings in a lawsuit. The lawsuit is *Bass v. Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center*. It is being heard in a federal court and in a Texas state court at the same time.

When lawyers file papers in court, they must tell the truth — about the facts, about what the other side's papers say, and about what past court rulings held. This guide lists places where a filing did not do that.

**How to read this guide.** Each entry has a short code (like F-01 for a federal filing or S-03 for a state filing). For each one you will see where the problem is, what happened in plain words, the exact words that were written, why it matters, and how it was checked.

**This was tested fairly.** Before any item went on this list, the strongest honest defense of the wording was written out and tested against the real record. Only items that still failed that test are here. Every item also quotes the exact words that were filed and names the source, so anyone can check it for themselves.

**This is a draft.** It has not been published yet. A companion document — the detailed candor catalog — gives the full legal version of every item, with case citations.

---

## Part 1 — The Federal Court Filings

### F-01 — a very serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 16 footnote 5.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers told the court that Mr. Bass's own court papers told about his conduct using words like 'bodily fluids,' 'diarrhea,' and 'vomit.' Those words aren't in his court papers at all. They appear only in documents the defendants themselves attached to their motion.

**What they actually wrote:**

> communications sent directly to faculty members involving bodily fluids, and (iii) vague criticism of COVID-19

**Why this matters:** A motion to dismiss is judged on what the plaintiff's own papers actually say. By putting the defendants' words into Mr. Bass's papers, the filing makes his case look like something he didn't write. The judge could rule against him based on words he never used.

**How we know:** We searched every version of Mr. Bass's complaint for those words. They don't appear. We then found the same words in the defendants' Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 8. That is where the description really came from.

---

### F-02 — a very serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 17 body text.

**What happened:** The filing pointed the court to Exhibit 4 to support a claim. Exhibit 4 is a two-page university policy. The filing cited pages that don't exist in it, and the words the filing said were on those pages don't appear anywhere in that exhibit.

**What they actually wrote:**

> approved university process.” See TTUHSC OP 77.14, Establishing Reasonable Accommodations for Students with Disabilities, attached as Exhibit 4, at pp. 1-2.

**Why this matters:** When a filing cites a document, the judge trusts that the document says what the filing claims. Here the cited pages aren't real. The judge could rely on support that isn't there.

**How we know:** We read all of Exhibit 4. It is only two pages long. We searched it for the quoted phrase, and the phrase isn't in it. We also checked the other exhibits in the same motion and didn't find it.

---

### F-03 — a very serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 3 footnote 2 + accompanying text.

**What happened:** The filing told about Exhibit 1 as the notice that told Mr. Bass about his hearing. Exhibit 1 is a different document, with a different name and a different date. The real hearing notice is Exhibit 2.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff was first notified of the consolidated board hearing on November 9, 2023 and a week later he received a second hearing notice informing him the hearing would be held on December 11.

**Why this matters:** The dates and the documents matter for whether Mr. Bass got fair notice of his hearing. Mixing up the two exhibits changes the timeline the judge sees.

**How we know:** We compared the filing's description to the actual exhibits. Exhibit 1 is titled 'Notice of Consolidation of Outstanding Student Matters' and is dated November 9, 2023. Exhibit 2 is the hearing notice, dated November 16, 2023.

---

### F-30 — a very serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at Throughout.

**What happened:** After the defendants filed their motion, Mr. Bass filed a response on the court docket that listed the false statements in it. Fifteen days later, the defendants filed a reply. The reply repeated the same factual claims without correcting them, even though the objections were already on the record.

**What they actually wrote:**

> these reasons, and those set forth in Defendants’ Motion, Defendants respectfully request that the Court grant their Motion to Dismiss in its entirety and dismiss Plaintiff’s claims with prejudice.

**Why this matters:** Once a lawyer is told that a statement is false, repeating it is more serious than making it the first time. Here the repetition happened with the objections already filed and known.

**How we know:** We checked the docket dates. Mr. Bass's response listing the misstatements was filed February 15, 2026. The defendants' reply was filed March 2, 2026, fifteen days later, and repeated the same claims.

---

### F-74 — a very serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at p. 13.

**What happened:** The reply cited 1 Texas Administrative Code § 57.1(12). That subsection doesn't exist. Section 57.1 ends at subsection (10). The right subsection is (6). Subsection (6) defines "Outside Counsel" as a lawyer or law firm chosen by an agency to provide legal services. It also rules out "a full-time employee of the Agency or the Office of the Attorney General." On its face, subsection (6) sorts Mr. Gibson into a category the AG doesn't defend.

**What they actually wrote:**

> counsel and full-time government employees for administrative purposes. See, e.g., 1 Tex. Admin. Code § 57.1(12). They do not address litigation authority, conflicts of interest, or the propriety of

**Why this matters:** Citing a subsection that doesn't exist is serious because the reader can't check the text. The real controlling subsection -- (6) -- has language that defeats the reply's point.

**How we know:** We pulled the current text of 1 Texas Administrative Code § 57.1. It has subsections (1) through (10). Subsection (6) carries the "Outside Counsel" definition the reply skipped.

---

### F-04 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 12 (citing Ex. 9).

**What happened:** The filing cited the student handbook as the 2024-2025 edition. The handbook actually attached as Exhibit 9 is the 2023-2024 edition. Mr. Bass's conduct happened in November 2023, so the earlier edition is the one that applies.

**What they actually wrote:**

> See TTUHSC Student Handbook, Code of Professional Conduct, 2024-2025, attached as Exhibit 9, at p. 17.

**Why this matters:** The right edition of the handbook controls what rules Mr. Bass had to follow. Citing a later edition can hide the speech protections in the version that was actually in force at the time.

**How we know:** We checked the cover page of Exhibit 9. It reads '2023-2024.' The filing's citation says '2024-2025.' The two don't match.

---

### F-05 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 9.

**What happened:** The filing said Mr. Bass never claimed he asked for disability help before his hearing. He did. His papers say so. They describe written notice of a disability. They describe requests to the disability office. Both happened before the hearing.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff provides no evidence or claim that prior to submitting his request to SDS in the

**Why this matters:** Whether he asked, and when, is central to his disability claims. Erasing the claim ends part of the case before any proof is weighed.

**How we know:** We read the relevant paragraphs of the amended complaint. Paragraph 25 says he gave written notice and asked the disability office for help before the December 11 hearing. Exhibit 8 also notes his ADHD diagnosis.

---

### F-06 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 14.

**What happened:** The filing said Mr. Bass never identified a specific false statement made by a specific person. His court papers do identify them. They name dates, recipients, and, in one paragraph, the person who wrote the message.

**What they actually wrote:**

> however, plead the publication of a materially false statement by any specific Defendant, as

**Why this matters:** A defamation claim needs a specific statement and a specific speaker. Saying those details are missing, when they are in the papers, can get the claim dismissed for no real reason.

**How we know:** We read the paragraphs of the amended complaint that the filing was answering. They list specific messages with dates and recipients, and one names Rachel Forbes as the author.

---

### F-07 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at pp. 15-16.

**What happened:** The filing said Mr. Bass's papers don't point to any specific speech that led to the discipline against him. His papers do. They describe a November 3, 2023 social-media post and quote its exact words.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Here, Plaintiff’s own pleading fails to identify with any specificity what speech allegedly triggered the challenged disciplinary actions.

**Why this matters:** His case is partly about being punished for speech. If the court is told no specific speech was identified, a free-speech claim can be dismissed even though the speech is named in the papers.

**How we know:** We read paragraph 31A of the amended complaint. It describes the November 3, 2023 post by date and content. The complaint also quotes the post word for word.

---

### F-08 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 18.

**What happened:** The filing said there were no specific claims that any of the individuals acted out of a wish to retaliate. The court papers do make those claims. Several paragraphs describe named people urging Mr. Bass to stop his online speech.

**What they actually wrote:**

> There are no specific allegations that any of the individuals had any retaliatory animus against Plaintiff's allegedly protected speech.

**Why this matters:** A retaliation claim depends on showing the people involved had a retaliatory motive. Saying that claim is absent, when it is in the papers, removes the heart of the claim.

**How we know:** We read the paragraphs the filing was responding to. They describe specific named people taking specific actions tied to Mr. Bass's speech.

---

### F-09 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at pp. 8, 12-13.

**What happened:** The filing told about Mr. Bass's hearing as one where he had a lawyer and presented his side. His court papers describe a hearing with serious limits. They say the hearing officer blocked objections, required questions in writing, cut his questioning short, and limited his witnesses.

**What they actually wrote:**

> was represented by counsel, and presented his position. See Complaint, ¶¶ 25-30, 42.

**Why this matters:** Whether the hearing was fair is a key question in the case. Telling it as normal, while leaving out the limits Mr. Bass pleaded, hides the very facts his claim rests on.

**How we know:** We read the amended-complaint paragraphs that describe the hearing. They list specific restrictions placed on Mr. Bass during it.

---

### F-10 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 14.

**What happened:** The filing argued that Mr. Bass didn't describe the kind of public, status-changing harm his claim requires. His court papers do describe it. They set out four separate public actions that changed his standing, including a campus ban, a criminal trespass warning, and a notice of dismissal.

**What they actually wrote:**

> City of Garland, 204 F.3d 223, 226-28 (5th Cir. 2000) (stigma-plus requires publication of false and stigmatizing charges in connection with a change of legal status; if the statement is not false, the claim fails); see also Codd v.

**Why this matters:** This type of claim needs a false public charge tied to a change in legal status. Telling the court those facts are missing, when four are pleaded, can end the claim early.

**How we know:** We read paragraphs 34, 34A, 35, and 35A of the amended complaint. Each describes a separate public action affecting Mr. Bass's status.

---

### F-11 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at pp. 3-4.

**What happened:** On a motion to dismiss, the court is supposed to look at the plaintiff's own papers. Here the filing told about the misconduct complaints against Mr. Bass in detail. His papers mention those complaints but don't describe what they said. The detailed description came from the defendants' own exhibits.

**What they actually wrote:**

> The four complaints of misconduct included: (1) unprofessional conduct by expressing romantic feelings toward a resident, (2) unprofessional conduct by sending photos of his own diarrhea and vomit to the clerkship director and Assistant Vice Dean, (3) unprofessional conduct by entering

**Why this matters:** A motion to dismiss tests the plaintiff's papers, not the defendant's evidence. Bringing in outside material lets the defendants argue their version of the facts before any evidence is tested.

**How we know:** We read the complaint paragraphs that mention the misconduct complaints. They don't describe the contents. We found the detailed description in the defendants' Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 8.

---

### F-12 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 7.

**What happened:** The filing stated as fact that Mr. Bass never again asked about the status of his application. That statement isn't in his court papers. It was added to the motion with no source in the pleadings.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff never again inquired about the application's status.

**Why this matters:** A motion to dismiss must stay within the plaintiff's papers. Adding a new fact that helps the defendants asks the judge to accept something that hasn't been pleaded or proven.

**How we know:** We searched the amended complaint for any statement that Mr. Bass stopped asking about his application. There is none. The claim appears only in the defendants' motion.

---

### F-13 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 9.

**What happened:** The filing said Mr. Bass had three years to ask for disability help and didn't. His papers say the opposite. He gave written notice of a disability. He asked the disability services office for help. He did this near the events, not years late.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Arguably Plaintiff had three years to request disability accommodations.

**Why this matters:** Timing matters for a disability claim. Calling him years late flips the timeline he pleaded.

**How we know:** We read paragraph 25 of the amended complaint. It says he gave the notice and made the requests before the December 11, 2023 hearing.

---

### F-14 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at pp. 3-6.

**What happened:** The filing said it could rely on its attached exhibits under a rule that lets courts consider documents the complaint refers to. Two of its exhibits go beyond that rule. They give the defendants' own account of disputed events, which the complaint neither attached nor relied on.

**What they actually wrote:**

> FACTUAL BACKGROUND1

**Why this matters:** The rule the filing cited is narrow. Using it to bring in the defendants' version of contested facts stretches a limited rule into a way to argue the merits early.

**How we know:** We checked the rule the filing cited and then reviewed Exhibit 8 and Exhibit 9. Those exhibits contain the defendants' descriptions of the complaints, the hearing, and Mr. Bass's conduct, which fall outside the narrow rule.

---

### F-16 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at Pages 2-3 n.1 vs. rest of brief.

**What happened:** Early in the motion, the filing told the court it would only consider the complaint and a few closely related documents. Later in the same motion, it brought in misconduct details from an exhibit the complaint didn't rely on. The motion doesn't follow the rule it set for itself.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Footnote 1 invokes Funk v. Stryker Corp. / Lone Star Fund V. (U.S.), L.P. v. Barclays Bank PLC for the 'incorporated by reference' standard - i.e., the court may consider documents 'incorporated into the complaint by reference.' Yet by p. 3 the brief introduces misconduct detail from Exhibit 2 that is NOT incorporated by reference into the FAC (no FAC paragraph cites Ex. 2); by p. 16 it fabricates a Complaint citation (Item 1).

**Why this matters:** A filing should hold to the standard it tells the court it is using. Setting one rule and then breaking it lets the defendants argue facts the rule was meant to keep out.

**How we know:** We compared footnote 1 of the motion with its later pages. Footnote 1 states the narrow standard. The later pages import misconduct allegations from Exhibit 2, which falls outside that standard.

---

### F-17 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at pp. 4-5, 12-13.

**What happened:** The filing told about the person who ran Mr. Bass's hearing as a neutral hearing officer. It didn't tell the court that the same person was a paid lawyer for the university, under contracts worth more than $393,000. One of Mr. Bass's claims is built on that relationship.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Hearing Officer. See TTUHSC’s Hearing Process and Rules of Decorum, dated December 11,

**Why this matters:** Whether the hearing officer was independent goes to whether the hearing was fair. Leaving out his paid ties to the university hides a fact directly tied to Mr. Bass's claim.

**How we know:** We checked the outside-counsel contracts between the hearing officer and the university. They show eight contracts and more than $393,000 in payments. None of this is mentioned in the motion.

---

### F-24 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at pp. 3-4.

**What happened:** The filing stated that the complaints against Mr. Bass were filed within a set date range. The defendants' own Exhibit 8 lists one of those complaints with a date outside that range. The motion's date window doesn't match its own exhibit.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Between August 1, 2023 and October 27, 2023, three (3) Student Code of Conduct complaints were filed against Plaintiff, and Plaintiff lodged six (6)

**Why this matters:** The timeline of the complaints matters to the case. A date window that conflicts with the defendants' own document can mislead the court about when events happened.

**How we know:** We compared the date range in the motion to the dates in Exhibit 8. Exhibit 8 lists a grievance dated November 10, 2023, which falls outside the range the motion gave.

---

### F-27 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 5.

**What happened:** The filing cited the part of the conduct code that covers forwarding a report to the dean. It cited the wrong subsection. The defendants' own Exhibit 8 cites the correct one.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Pursuant to the Code of Conduct, Part II.F.4.o, the Report was then forwarded to the Dean of the School of Medicine, Dr.

**Why this matters:** Citing the right rule matters when the filing is telling how the process is supposed to work. A wrong citation, contradicted by the defendants' own exhibit, can confuse which step actually applied.

**How we know:** We checked the conduct code and Exhibit 8. The forwarding step is Part II.F.4.n. Exhibit 8 cites II.F.4.n. The motion cites II.F.4.o.

---

### F-31 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion for Leave to File SAC (Doc. 48), at pp. 3-4.

**What happened:** The filing said Mr. Bass's revised complaint adds no new legal theories. It does. It is reorganized into seven counts. It adds a new defendant. It adds a separate claim against another defendant on a new ground.

**What they actually wrote:**

> proposed amendment “does not add new legal theories” and that “[t]he claims asserted are the

**Why this matters:** The court weighs what the changes are. Calling them nothing, when they are real, can kill the request on a false premise.

**How we know:** We compared the two complaints. The revised one has seven counts, adds Defendant Trotter, and adds a separate count against Defendant Gibson on quasi-judicial-immunity grounds.

---

### F-38 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at pp. 5-6.

**What happened:** The filing said the Fifth Circuit limits who can move to disqualify. The case it cited says the opposite. That case calls a disqualification motion the right way for a party in the case to raise conflict-of-interest issues.

**What they actually wrote:**

> A non-client movant must demonstrate a concrete, particularized risk that the alleged conflict will prejudice the fairness of

**Why this matters:** Telling the court a binding ruling says one thing when it says the other can shut down a valid motion at the start. The court trusts lawyers to state the law right.

**How we know:** We read In re American Airlines. It says a motion to disqualify is the right method for a party to bring conflict-of-interest issues to the court.

---

### F-40 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at pp. 4-5.

**What happened:** The filing said disqualification fails because the motion rests on a future, not a present, conflict. The Supreme Court case the filing itself cited says the opposite. It says "potential" conflicts are the more common situation where a court can act.

**What they actually wrote:**

> fails because it rests entirely on speculation, not an actual, present conflict.

**Why this matters:** Citing a Supreme Court case and leaving out the part that cuts against you changes how the law looks. The Court told judges to watch for potential conflicts, not just present ones.

**How we know:** We read the Wheat case the filing itself cited. It says the district court has wide latitude in conflict rulings in "rare cases where an actual conflict" is shown and in "the more common cases where a potential for conflict exists."

---

### F-43 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at p. 11.

**What happened:** The filing cited Filarsky for the rule that one lawyer can represent both the institution and a paid outside contractor. Filarsky is about a different question. It is about whether a private contractor can raise qualified immunity. It says nothing about who must serve as counsel. The same lawyer also didn't raise the Filarsky qualified-immunity defense for the contractor when it would have helped.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377, 389–90 (2012) (qualified immunity analysis focuses on the nature

**Why this matters:** A case used to defeat disqualification should speak to representation. A defense that helps a client should be raised when it helps, not held back.

**How we know:** We read Filarsky. It holds that a private contractor may raise qualified immunity. It doesn't address counsel choice. We then checked the 33-page motion to dismiss. It doesn't raise the Filarsky defense on Gibson's behalf.

---

### F-46 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at p. 7 (and p. 11).

**What happened:** The filing said the institution hasn't argued that the contractor acted outside his engagement. It said it hasn't raised any defense that would put liability on him. That is the very pattern Mr. Bass's motion names. The institution isn't raising the contractor's strongest defenses because that would harm the institution. The filing offers the concession as a denial.

**What they actually wrote:**

> TTUHSC has not argued that Gibson acted outside the scope of any engagement, nor has it advanced any defense that would impose liability

**Why this matters:** When the same lawyer has two clients with conflicting interests, the warning sign is missing arguments. Saying so plainly, while framing it as a defense, confirms the conflict the motion names.

**How we know:** We read the cited passages at pages 7 and 11 of the response. They describe a "unified" presentation in which the institution doesn't raise the contractor-specific defenses. That matches the Dunton pattern.

---

### F-49 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at Throughout the 18-page Response.

**What happened:** Mr. Bass's motion to disqualify expressly raised the question of whether the joint clients had consented to the joint representation after a proper consultation. The defendants had three weeks and an eighteen-page response to address it. The response didn't address it. Texas conduct rules require that consent come only after consultation.

**What they actually wrote:**

> materials, and administrative definitions to suggest that the Attorney General’s representation of Defendant Gibson is improper.

**Why this matters:** When consent is the dispositive question, silence on it is itself an answer. A response that has the time and space to show consent, and doesn't, leaves the conflict standing.

**How we know:** We read the motion (Doc. 46 at 13-14), which placed consent in issue. We then read the entire eighteen-page response. It doesn't show that consent was got after consultation, as Tex. Disciplinary R. Prof'l Conduct 1.06(c) and comment 8 require.

---

### F-51 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at p. 2.

**What happened:** The defendants' reply brief said Mr. Bass had three chances to fix his complaint and missed all three. The record shows only one prior amendment. There were no three chances. The count was wrong.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff challenges a completed student dismissal decision, which he appealed and was denied, and seeks retrospective relief tied to past

**Why this matters:** Repeated-failure-to-cure is a real bar to leave to amend. But it needs a real count. Three chances when there was one is a fact the judge would rely on if not flagged.

**How we know:** We pulled the docket. The complaint was filed and amended once. The defendants' reply at page 12 lists three. We compared the two and found the count doesn't match.

---

### F-53 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at pp. 7-8.

**What happened:** The reply quoted Pickett for the rule that a state agency is immune. Pickett does say that. The reply left out the next sentence in Pickett. That sentence carves out a narrow class of claims. Mr. Bass's claims fit the carve-out.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff submitted a disability accommodation request one business day before the dismissal hearing. Institutional policy required review and approval through the Student Disability Services office before accommodations could issue. No Letter of Accommodation had been granted at the time of the hearing.

**Why this matters:** Selective quotation hides the part of the rule that helps the other side. Here the missing sentence is the part Mr. Bass needs.

**How we know:** We pulled Pickett, 37 F.4th 1013, and read the full paragraph at page 1025. The reply quoted the first sentence. The next sentence carves out claims for prospective relief against state officers.

---

### F-54 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at pp. 3-4.

**What happened:** The filing told the court that Mr. Bass hadn't identified any binding precedent supporting his name-clearing argument. He had already cited that precedent in a response filed earlier on the docket, including a Fifth Circuit decision involving this same institution. The defendants' reply was filed after his response and still treated the precedent as absent.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff identifies no controlling precedent clearly establishing: (1) a right to a name-

**Why this matters:** Saying authority is missing when it is on the docket can lead the court to dismiss a claim for an absence that isn't real. The fact that the response came after the precedent was cited makes the gap notice-based, not accidental.

**How we know:** We checked the docket. Mr. Bass's response (R2MTD, Doc. 33) cites controlling Fifth Circuit name-clearing authority, including Pickett v. TTUHSC. Doc. 38 was filed after Doc. 33 and still says that no controlling precedent was identified.

---

### F-56 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at p. 8.

**What happened:** The filing called a proposed pleading a "Proposed Third Amended Complaint." It wasn't a third pleading. It was a swap inside an open request to amend. The label makes the count look higher and the history more aggressive.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Amend/Correct” his prior motion and attached a Proposed Third Amended Complaint—

**Why this matters:** Calling a routine swap a "third" pleading hints at repeated failed tries. The court could weigh that against Mr. Bass for a posture that didn't happen.

**How we know:** We checked the docket. Doc. 32 was a swap of the proposed Second Amended Complaint inside the open leave-to-amend motion (Doc. 26). It wasn't a third pleading.

---

### F-57 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at p. 6.

**What happened:** The reply said the campus ban and the criminal trespass warning were the same act. They aren't. The campus ban came from the dean. The criminal trespass warning came from the campus police. They were issued separately.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Moreover, any “online backlash” Plaintiff received was clearly due to his

**Why this matters:** Two separate acts mean two separate harms. Treating them as one collapses Mr. Bass's standing claim into a single event when the papers plead two.

**How we know:** We read the amended complaint. The campus ban is at paragraph 34. The criminal trespass warning is at paragraph 34A. The defendants' own Exhibit 8 confirms they came from different offices.

---

### F-58 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at p. 6.

**What happened:** The filing said the only fair reading of Mr. Bass's pleading is that his post caused a disruption. The pleading says the opposite. It says the post was a brief reflection. It didn't name the institution. It didn't name any person. It didn't call for or threaten violence. The pleading also says the institution kept treating him in ways that don't fit a safety risk.

**What they actually wrote:**

> It is clear from Plaintiff's First Amended Complaint that the reasonable interpretation of the Plaintiff's statements caused a disruption.

**Why this matters:** On a motion to dismiss, the court reads the pleading in the plaintiff's favor. Calling one reading the only fair one, when the pleading says otherwise, flips the test.

**How we know:** We read paragraphs 31A, 31B, and 31C of the amended complaint. They describe the post's content, the lack of a threat, and ordinary meetings the institution held with Mr. Bass during the same time.

---

### F-62 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at p. 3.

**What happened:** The reply cited Verizon Md. v. Public Service Commission, 535 U.S. 635, 645 (2002), to argue that Ex parte Young doesn't apply. Page 645 of Verizon Md. says the test for Young is a "straightforward inquiry" into whether the complaint alleges an ongoing violation of federal law and asks for forward-looking relief. The Supreme Court used that page to describe how easy the test is to meet.

**What they actually wrote:**

> See Verizon Md., Inc. v. Pub. Serv. Comm’n of Md., 535 U.S. 635, 645 (2002).

**Why this matters:** A pincite is supposed to point to the page that supports the rule. Pointing to the page that says the opposite, without flagging the conflict, inverts the cited authority.

**How we know:** We pulled the Verizon Md. opinion. The "straightforward inquiry" language is on page 645, in the form the reply quoted on the opposite side.

---

### F-66 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion for Leave to File SAC (Doc. 48), at pp. 1-2 and p. 4.

**What happened:** The reply said Mr. Bass conceded he wasn't raising new legal theories. It called that decisive. Doc. 43 paragraphs 3 and 5 do mention the same theories. The same paragraphs also say more. They say the proposed Second Amended Complaint adds Mr. Trotter as a new defendant. They say it adds qualified-immunity pleading not in the current complaint. They say it reorders the counts for Rule 8. The reply quoted only the theory line and left out the rest.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff concedes that he is not asserting new legal theories and instead reorganizes the same claims already at issue. That concession is decisive.

> Even where notice may be inferred through shared counsel, relation back still requires a qualifying “mistake” concerning identity, which

**Why this matters:** Relation-back analysis is supposed to follow the current Supreme Court framework. Applying the older test after Krupski directed courts to ask a different question uses a rule that no longer controls.

**How we know:** We read both opinions. Krupski at 553-54 expressly directs the inquiry to what the new defendant knew.

### F-65 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion for Leave to File SAC (Doc. 48), at pp. 6-7.

The original Complaint at Doc. 1 named "Doe Hearing Officer 1, Does 2-10." The First Amended Complaint at paragraph 27A identifies Mr. Trotter by name, title, and conduct. **What they actually wrote:**

> The events giving rise to Plaintiff's claims occurred in late 2023, and the addition of Trotter falls outside the applicable limitations period unless relation back applies.

**Why this matters:** Relation back has more than one route. Leaving out the Doe-substitution route makes the limitations argument look stronger than the rule allows.

**How we know:** We read Doc. 1 (the original Complaint), which named "Doe Hearing Officer 1, Does 2-10." We read paragraph 27A of the First Amended Complaint, which identifies Mr. Trotter.

That keeps the policy question alive. Third, the structural conflict the motion names doesn't turn on the Monell label.

> Monell addressed liability of local governmental entities under Section 1983 and does

**Why this matters:** Citing Monell and Will to clear away the policy question leaves out three other ways the question stays in the case.

### F-71 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at p. 5 and p. 6.

**What happened:** The reply cited FDIC v. U.S. Fire, 50 F.3d 1304, 1313-14 (5th Cir. 1995), for the rule that a non-client can't invoke Texas Disciplinary Rules. U.S. Fire is more limited. Federal courts aren't bound by state rules. They may apply them under federal supervisory authority. In re American Airlines holds that party-litigants are the right movants for conflict-of-interest issues. The reply doesn't address that holding.

**What they actually wrote:**

> the Texas Disciplinary Rules are “guidelines” that do not create substantive rights enforceable by opposing parties. U.S. Fire Ins. Co., 50 F.3d at 1313–14. A non-client litigant cannot invoke those

**Why this matters:** When one case closes a door that another binding case opens, both have to be addressed. Leaving out the American Airlines holding makes the bar look firmer than the rule supports.

**How we know:** We read U.S. Fire at 1313-14 and In re American Airlines at 611. American Airlines confirms party-litigant standing under federal supervisory authority.

### F-72 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at p. 4 and p. 14.

**What happened:** The reply cited Galderma Labs. v. Actavis Mid Atl. LLC, 927 F. Supp. 2d 390, 394-95 (N.D. Tex. 2013), for the rule that applies here. Galderma is a current-client conflict case. The law firm in Galderma was representing both Galderma and Actavis at the same time when the suit was filed. The opinion turned on whether prospective written informed consent under Model Rule 1.7(a)(2) was enough. That posture doesn't match a case where one set of lawyers represents an institution and a co-defendant contractor at the same time, with no informed consent.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Galderma Labs., L.P. v. Actavis Mid Atl. LLC, 927 F. Supp. 2d 390, 394-95 (N.D. Tex. 2013).

**Why this matters:** The doctrinal posture changes what the case decides. Borrowing a current-client informed-consent rule for a co-defendant joint-representation problem with no consent applies a rule from a different fact pattern.

**How we know:** We read Galderma at 394-95. The opinion turns on prospective written informed consent under Model Rule 1.7(a)(2), in a current-client situation.

### F-73 — a moderate concern

**What happened:** The motion to disqualify said Tex. Ethics Op. 579 doesn't apply here. Op. 579 says that a "unit of government" counts as a law firm for the imputation rule. The hearing officer is a unit-of-government lawyer. Op. 579 applies directly.

**Why this matters:** Op. 579 is the controlling Texas ethics opinion on the imputation rule. Saying it doesn't apply, when the opinion's text matches the facts here, sidelines the rule that decides the issue.

**How we know:** We pulled Tex. Ethics Op. 579 from the Texas Center for Legal Ethics. We read its text. The phrase "unit of government" appears and is defined to include university lawyers acting in that role.

### F-78 — a moderate concern

> Pistikopoulos lacks standing to complain about the Attorney General's representation of Vestal in this matter because he has no 'legally protected interest' in the identity of Vestal's counsel.

**Why this matters:** Will and Hafer together draw the line between official and individual capacity. The reply quoted only one half and used it as if it were the whole rule.

**How we know:** We pulled Will v. Michigan, 491 U.S. 58, and Hafer v. Melo, 502 U.S. 21. We read the full paragraphs at Hafer page 25. The reply quoted the first sentence. The next sentence carves out individual-capacity suits.

### F-79 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at pp. 4-5.

**What happened:** The reply called Woods v. Covington County Bank, 537 F.2d 804 (5th Cir. 1976), and Kitchin "earlier decisions" and treated In re American Airlines as the controlling later case that has displaced them. Neither Woods nor Kitchin has been overruled. The panel in American Airlines expressly applies Woods. The supersession is invented.

**What they actually wrote:**

> earlier decisions such as Woods v. Covington County Bank, 537 F.2d 804 (5th Cir. 1976), and

**Why this matters:** Calling cases "earlier" and pointing to a later case as "controlling" suggests the earlier cases no longer apply. When the later case is in fact still applying the earlier ones, the framing misleads about the doctrinal posture.

### F-80 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at Multiple (pp. 4, 5, 6, 7, 15).

**What happened:** The reply cited Horaist v. Doctor's Hospital of Opelousas, 255 F.3d 261, 266 (5th Cir. 2001), five times for a "balancing of interests" framework. Horaist analyzed disqualification under Texas Rule 1.09. Rule 1.09 governs former-client conflicts. The motion here uses Rule 1.06(f). Rule 1.06(f) governs current-client conflicts and imputation. The two rules use different tests.

**What they actually wrote:**

> preserve the integrity of the judicial process. American Airlines, 972 F.2d at 611; Horaist v. Doctor’s Hosp. of Opelousas, 255 F.3d 261, 266 (5th Cir. 2001).

**Why this matters:** Rule 1.09's balancing test comes from former-client facts. It weighs different interests than the current-client and imputation test in Rule 1.06(f). Treating the two as one elides the split.

**How we know:** We read Horaist at 266. It analyzes a former-client conflict under Rule 1.09. The motion's framework is Rule 1.06(f).

### F-83 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at pp. 1-2 and p. 4.

**What happened:** The reply pointed to a state immunity rule for federal civil rights claims. State immunity rules don't govern Section 1983 claims. The federal-immunity rules do. The reply used the wrong body of law for the claims at issue.

**What they actually wrote:**

> That authority, however, is sharply limited: disqualification is “a severe sanction” that must be used sparingly and only when necessary to

**Why this matters:** Section 1983 has its own immunity framework. Bringing in state immunity changes the test the court applies.

**How we know:** We pulled the state-law cite from the reply and the federal-immunity cases for Section 1983. The two bodies of law point in different directions on this question.

### F-84 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at pp. 2, 8, 9, 15.

**What happened:** The reply said four times that the defendants have "aligned defenses." The list includes sovereign immunity. Under Hafer v. Melo, 502 U.S. at 25-26, sovereign immunity is not a defense for a person sued in his own name. Mr. Gibson is sued only in his own name. So that defense isn't his.

**What they actually wrote:**

> counsel and asserted aligned defenses, including sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, and failure to state a claim.

**Why this matters:** Saying it four times doesn't fix a flaw. A Supreme Court rule defeats the claim.

**How we know:** We checked all four uses of the "aligned defenses" line. We checked Hafer at 25-26. We checked the dismissal motions. The Hafer rule applies here.

### F-85 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 10 footnote 4.

**What happened:** Footnote 6 of Doc. 27 cited Esfeller v. O'Keefe as a binding immunity case. Esfeller is unpublished. Under Fifth Circuit Rule 47.5.4, unpublished cases aren't binding. The footnote used Esfeller as if it were. It also left out a published case called Shamloo, which came out the other way.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Notably, after filing the First Amended Complaint, Plaintiff affirmatively withdrew "any request for temporary or preliminary injunctive relief," including the request embedded in the Complaint. See Plaintiff's Response to the Findings, Conclusions, and Recommendation, ECF No. 24 at 1-2. [. . .] and independently defeats standing for prospective relief under Article III and Ex parte Young.

**Why this matters:** Binding vs. persuasive controls the weight a case gets. Using an unpublished case as binding and skipping the published case against you stacks the deck.

**How we know:** We pulled Esfeller v. O'Keefe and confirmed it is unpublished. We pulled Fifth Circuit Rule 47.5.4 and read the binding-status rule. We pulled Shamloo and confirmed it is published and comes out for the plaintiff.

### F-86 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at p. 19 footnote 6.

**What happened:** Footnote 6 strung together two cases for qualified immunity on a First Amendment higher-education claim. The cases are Esfeller v. O'Keefe, 391 F. App'x 337 (5th Cir. 2010), and Shamloo v. Mississippi State Board, 620 F.2d 516 (5th Cir. 1980). Three problems stack. First, Esfeller is unpublished. Under 5th Cir. Rule 47.5.4, unpublished opinions after 1996 aren't precedent. So they can't set "clearly established law" for qualified immunity. The footnote treats Esfeller as binding anyway. Second, Shamloo was a plaintiff's win. The Fifth Circuit applied Tinker and struck down the university regulations. The case cuts against the defense. Third, Esfeller was about a harassment pattern by an undergraduate. The case here is a single off-campus social-media post by a graduate student. The facts don't match.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Circuit and other circuit courts have applied Tinker to First Amendment higher education cases. [. . .] For example, in Esfeller v. O’Keefe, the Fifth Circuit held that the university’s Code of Conduct that limited speech that “intrudes upon … the rights of other students,” was not facially unconstitutional under Tinker. 391 F. App’x 337, 341 (5th Cir. 2010). As a result, Plaintiff cannot establish that the Individual Defendants personally violated clearly established law in taking action against Plaintiff due to his threatening social media post. [. . .] See Esfeller v. O’Keefe, 391 F. App’x 337, 341-42 (5th Cir. 2010); Shamloo v. Mississippi State Bd. of Tr. of Insts. of Higher Learning, 620 F.2d 516, 521–24 (5th Cir. 1980); Students for Justice in Palestine, at the University of Houston, et al. v. Abbott, Case No. 1:24-cv-00523-RP, ECF 62, at 11 (W.D. Tex. Oct. 28, 2024) (applying Tinker to dismiss claims on qualified immunity grounds).

**Why this matters:** A clearly-set-law test needs binding precedent on point. An unpublished Fifth Circuit opinion isn't binding. A plaintiff's-win case isn't support for a defense outcome. And a harassment-pattern case isn't a match for a single-post case.

**How we know:** We read 5th Cir. Rule 47.5.4. We read the Esfeller opinion and its facts. We read Shamloo at 521-24. The Shamloo court struck down the regulations under Tinker.

**Where:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27), at Throughout.

**What happened:** The filing cited Pickett v. TTUHSC for an immunity rule and didn't note that the case includes language carving out the very class of claims Mr. Bass brings. The carve-out is in Pickett at page 1025.

**What they actually wrote:**

> No mention of Pickett v. TTUHSC, 37 F.4th 1013 (5th Cir. 2022).

**Why this matters:** Texas Disciplinary Rule 3.03(a)(4) tells lawyers to disclose controlling cases that hurt their side. The Pickett carve-out hurts the defendants' side here.

### F-41 — a minor concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50), at pp. 10-11 (three pages).

**What happened:** The filing pushed back on Mr. Bass's reliance on a decision called Dunton. The filing didn't mention the binding Fifth Circuit decision Dunton itself rests on, called Van Ooteghem. That earlier Fifth Circuit decision states that adverse interests in litigation require adverse legal counsel.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff’s Reliance on Out-of-Circuit Authority is Misplaced Plaintiff relies heavily on Dunton v.

**Why this matters:** Lawyers are expected to bring binding rulings to the court, including ones that an out-of-circuit case they are arguing about depends on. Omitting the local binding source keeps the court from seeing the controlling rule.

### F-52 — a minor concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38), at pp. 7-8.

**What happened:** The defendants' reply cited Pickett v. TTUHSC, 37 F.4th 1013, at pages 1032-33 for an immunity bar. The actual holding at those pages is narrower. Pickett at 1025 says sovereign immunity bars some claims. It does not say what the reply quoted.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff cites to Pickett v. Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center in his Response but fails to recognize the distinction between cases. Indeed, Plaintiff misreads Pickett and overlooks the Fifth Circuit's holding regarding the structured interactive process.

## Part 2 — The State Court Filings

### S-08 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at p. 4, § III.B.

**What happened:** The lawyers said Mr. Bass "controlled" the bad email (the missing "a" in "kbassphiladelphi[a]@gmail.com") through his own eFileTexas account. He didn't. The bad address lived in a different system. It lived in the county court's service-contacts list. His eFileTexas profile always had the right address.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff controlled his own eFileTexas account and received explicit notice that service to his email address was failing. Rather than correct the problem, he took no action.

**Why this matters:** This is a record claim that drives a key issue. Could he have fixed the address ahead of time? If he couldn't see or change the bad entry, blaming him for it is wrong on the facts.

**How we know:** His MNT attached Exhibit G. The exhibit is a screenshot of his eFileTexas profile. It shows the right address. The bad address lives in the county service-contacts list.

---

### State-09 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at p. 1 (Introduction); reiterated p. 4 § III.B.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers told the court a March 3, 2026 notification showed Mr. Bass 'the precise error in his email address.' It didn't. The notification went to his correct address. The bad entry was in a separate county-court contacts list he couldn't see.

**What they actually wrote:**

> On March 3, 2026, Plaintiff received system-generated notifications advising that service to him was undeliverable and identifying the precise error in his email address. That notice put Plaintiff on clear alert that his ability to receive filings in this case had been compromised.

**Why this matters:** The framing implies Mr. Bass had a clear warning the truncation was permanent and in his own profile. Neither was true. The misstatement is part of the same control conflation S-08 catches.

**How we know:** We read the March 3 notification language. It doesn't identify which system holds the bad address. Exhibit G to the MNT shows the address was correct on Mr. Bass's side of the system.

---

### State-11 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at p. 5, § III.D.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers told the court Mr. Bass's complaint was about losing a 'sur-reply opportunity.' It wasn't. The MNT says Mr. Bass received no notice of the Reply or of the Notice of Submission. He couldn't appear, file an objection, or be heard at all on the dispositive motion.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff's assertion that he did not receive Defendants' Reply or the Notice of Submission does not establish a constitutional violation. There is no right to file a sur-reply absent leave of court, and a movant may request submission without oral hearing. Plaintiff does not identify any argument he was prevented from making or any evidence he was unable to present.

**Why this matters:** Restating the harm as a smaller, lost-extra-brief harm changes the injury the court is being asked to remedy. The recharacterization makes the harm look minor.

**How we know:** The MNT itself identifies the harm as no notice of the Reply or the Notice of Submission, not lost-sur-reply. The 'sur-reply' framing in the defendants' brief inverts what Mr. Bass actually pleaded.

---

### State-15 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-02-09), at p. 5, § III.B.

**What happened:** The brief told the court that Mr. Bass is fighting his dismissal. He isn't. The petition says so on its face. It asks the court for two things only: that the school follow its own records-fix process, and that Mr. Bass get a name-clearing hearing.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Although Plaintiff characterizes this suit as a records-procedure dispute, the relief sought necessarily implicates TTUHSC's disciplinary dismissal and transcript notation. Academic discipline, transcript designations, and student status determinations are quintessential discretionary institutional judgments entitled to judicial deference.

**Why this matters:** If a court treats a case as a fight about the merits of a dismissal, it can throw the case out on academic-deference grounds. Those grounds have nothing to do with the duty to follow a records-fix process.

**How we know:** The petition says it doesn't challenge the dismissal. It asks only for records correction and a name-clearing hearing.

---

### State-22 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response to Plaintiff's Motion to Set Evidentiary Hearing (filed 2026-04-29), at p. 1 (intro); p. 2.

**What happened:** The brief told the court that the facts about notice 'aren't genuinely disputed.' The MNT fights every one of them. It fights what the March 3 e-mail showed. It fights who 'controlled' the bad address. It fights when Mr. Bass first knew of the March 26 ruling.

**What they actually wrote:**

> But Texas courts routinely resolve Rule 306a issues based on sworn filings, declarations, and the existing record where, as here, the relevant facts concerning notice and actual knowledge are not genuinely disputed. [. . .] Here, Plaintiff's own filings establish that he had actual notice that service to him was failing well before the Court's ruling and took no action to correct it.

**Why this matters:** Calling a fact 'undisputed' tells the court it can skip the fight and rule on what the brief assumes.

**How we know:** We checked the brief's words against the record. The MNT, Exhibit G, and the re:SearchTX docket each show a real fight on each point.

---

### State-23 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response to Plaintiff's Motion to Set Evidentiary Hearing (filed 2026-04-29), at Throughout — post-notice repetition.

**What happened:** The April 29 brief said the same wrong things again. It said Mr. Bass 'controlled' the bad e-mail. It said he had 'actual notice' of the March 3 issue. Mr. Bass's April 23 Reply had already shown why both were wrong. The brief came out six days later anyway.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Here, Plaintiff's own filings establish that he had actual notice that service to him was failing well before the Court's ruling and took no action to correct it.

**Why this matters:** Saying the same wrong thing twice — after the other side has shown it is wrong — turns a slip into a stance. Texas Disciplinary Rule 3.03(a)(1) and Rule 13 reach repeats with notice.

**How we know:** The re:SearchTX envelope IDs and timestamps show the Reply landed first. The April 29 brief repeats the same claims from Items S-08 and State-09.

---

### State-26 — a serious concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-03-18), at p. 4, § II.C (parenthetical cite).

**What happened:** The defendants said a parallel suit means abatement of the state suit. Texas abatement rules apply when both suits cover the same parties and the same claims. The two suits here don't. The federal suit has more parties and more claims.

**What they actually wrote:**

> See Southwestern Bell Telephone, L.P. v. Emmett, 459 S.W.3d 578 (Tex. 2015) (recognizing that statutory ‘shall’ language does not eliminate discretion where implementation requires judgment).

**Why this matters:** Abatement removes a case from a forum. A mismatched parallel doesn't trigger it. The defendants' rule would block a state suit any time a federal one was filed.

**How we know:** We compared the two pleadings. The state suit has the TTUHSC defendants only. The federal suit adds individual defendants and federal civil-rights claims the state court can't hear.

---

### S-03 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at p. 5, § III.D.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers quoted a U.S. Supreme Court case for the rule that due process is met when a party has 'a meaningful opportunity to present his case.' They left out what the case actually decided. The Court in Peralta v. Heights Medical Center reversed the lower court because notice failed.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Due process requires notice and an opportunity to be heard, not perfection in the mechanics of service. The United States Supreme Court has held that due process is satisfied where a party is afforded a meaningful opportunity to present his case. See Peralta v. Heights Med. Ctr., Inc., 485 U.S. 80, 84-86 (1988).

**Why this matters:** Quoting the standard a case states while hiding what the case decided makes the case look supportive when it isn't.

**How we know:** We read Peralta v. Heights Medical Center, 485 U.S. 80 (1988). Page 84 says 'Failure to give notice violates the most rudimentary demands of due process of law.' The brief left that sentence out.

---

### S-04 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at pp. 2-3, § III.A.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers cited Memorial Hospital v. Gillis for a 'reasonable inquiry' diligence rule. The case doesn't state that rule. Gillis held only that the moving party didn't prove the basic Rule 306a requirements in the trial court.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Texas courts have long held that Rule 306a does not protect a party who fails to exercise diligence after receiving information that would lead a reasonable person to inquire further. See Mem'l Hosp. v. Gillis, 741 S.W.2d 364, 365-66 (Tex. 1987).

**Why this matters:** Citing a case for a doctrine the case doesn't announce makes Texas law look like it carries a rule it doesn't.

**How we know:** We read Memorial Hospital v. Gillis, 741 S.W.2d 364 (Tex. 1987) (per curiam). The opinion doesn't contain the diligence language the brief attributes to it.

---

### S-05 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at pp. 3-4, §§ III.A and III.B.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers cited In re Lynd Co. for the idea that Rule 306a rarely extends deadlines. Lynd does the opposite. The Texas Supreme Court kept in place a trial court order that granted Rule 306a relief.

**What they actually wrote:**

> See, e.g., In re Lynd Co., 195 S.W.3d 682, 685 (Tex. 2006) (orig. proceeding) (explaining that Rule 306a relief depends on compliance with the rule's notice and timing requirements and does not extend deadlines absent the required showing)

**Why this matters:** Citing a case for a result the case rejected is a stronger form of mis-citation. The case's outcome cuts against the position the brief uses it to support.

**How we know:** We read In re Lynd Co., 195 S.W.3d 682 (Tex. 2006). The Texas Supreme Court conditionally granted mandamus to uphold a trial court's Rule 306a relief, at pages 684-85.

---

### S-06 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at p. 3, § III.A.

**What happened:** Same problem again. The defendants' lawyers cited John v. Marshall Health Services for the rule that Rule 306a relief is hard to get. The case actually reversed a court of appeals and held the movant's motion WAS timely.

**What they actually wrote:**

> John v. Marshall Health Servs., Inc., 58 S.W.3d 738, 741-42 (Tex. 2001) (per curiam) (explaining that Rule 306a extends deadlines only upon proof of late notice or actual knowledge as required by the rule).

**Why this matters:** This is the third case in a row cited for a rule the case rejected. A pattern of pincite-to-opposite-disposition citations is harder to explain as accidental.

**How we know:** We read John v. Marshall Health Services, 58 S.W.3d 738 (Tex. 2001) (per curiam). Pages 740-41 hold the Rule 306a(5) motion wasn't untimely; the case is favorable to 306a movants.

---

### State-13 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-03-18), at p. 4, § II.C.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers told the court that Houston Belt is a drainage-fee case and doesn't apply to internal academic policy. Houston Belt's actual rule is broader. A state official with discretion can still be sued for ultra-vires conduct when a statute also imposes constraints on that discretion.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Houston Belt involved a municipal ordinance defining the parameters of a drainage fee and statutory limits on its imposition. It did not involve internal academic policy governing record administration.

**Why this matters:** Reading a broad rule statement as fact-bound lets the defense skip past the rule that applies. The case isn't about drainage fees in the way that matters.

**How we know:** We read Houston Belt & Terminal Railway v. City of Houston, 487 S.W.3d 154 (Tex. 2016), at page 163. The Texas Supreme Court's rule statement isn't limited to drainage fees.

---

### State-14 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-03-18), at p. 4, § II.B (statutory text).

**What happened:** The brief summed up Tex. Gov't Code § 559.004 as if it only asked for a 'reasonable procedure.' The statute says more. It says the body 'shall correct or amend' wrong information. It must give a written reason if it says no. And it must let the person attach a statement.

**What they actually wrote:**

> The statute provides that a state governmental body "shall establish a reasonable procedure" under which an individual may seek correction of information and that the procedure "may not unduly burden" the individual. That language does not eliminate discretion. [. . .] By employing flexible terms such as "reasonable" and "unduly burden," the Legislature necessarily entrusted implementation to the governmental body.

**Why this matters:** Quoting only the soft words hides the parts that bind. The hard steps — correct, explain, attach — are what make this a procedural-duty case.

**How we know:** We read § 559.004. Subsections (b) and (c) carry the correct-or-explain duties the brief left out.

---

### State-16 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-02-09), at p. 5, § III.A + p. 6, § III.C (citing Heinrich).

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers cited City of El Paso v. Heinrich for the rule that ultra-vires suits are 'narrow.' That language is in Heinrich. The brief left out that Heinrich also reaches officials who exceed the constraints on their discretion, and that Houston Belt later confirmed and extended that part of Heinrich.

**What they actually wrote:**

> See City of El Paso v. Heinrich, 284 S.W.3d 366, 372-73 (Tex. 2009). [. . .] Plaintiff attempts to invoke the ultra vires exception to sovereign immunity. However, that exception is "narrow" and carefully circumscribed. See id. It permits prospective relief only where an official acts without legal authority or fails to perform a purely ministerial duty.

**Why this matters:** Citing the limiting half of a case while omitting the half that opens the door to liability misrepresents what the case allows. The omission is the candor issue.

**How we know:** We read Heinrich, 284 S.W.3d 366 (Tex. 2009), at page 372, and Houston Belt, 487 S.W.3d 154 (Tex. 2016), at page 163. Both confirm ultra-vires reaches statutory constraint violations.

---

### State-17 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-02-09), at p. 5, § III.B (academic-deference cluster).

**What happened:** The lawyers cited three cases for the rule that courts don't second-guess academic calls. The cases are Ewing, Than, and Alcorn. Each is about a challenge to a dismissal. Mr. Bass isn't challenging the dismissal. He is asking the court to enforce a records-correction duty.

**What they actually wrote:**

> See, e.g., Regents of Univ. of Mich. v. Ewing, 474 U.S. 214, 225 (1985) (courts should defer to academic decisions unless a substantial departure from accepted academic norms exists); University of Tex. Med. Sch. at Houston v. Than, 901 S.W.2d 926, 931 (Tex. 1995) (recognizing judicial reluctance to interfere with academic decision-making and institutional disciplinary determinations); see also Alcorn v. Vaksman, 877 S.W.2d 390, 403 (Tex. App.--Houston [1st Dist.] 1994, writ denied) (courts defer to academic judgments absent arbitrary or capricious action).

**Why this matters:** Using academic-deference cases against a duty claim shifts the test. It puts the plaintiff in a place where he can't win, no matter what the duty rule says.

**How we know:** We read Ewing, 474 U.S. 214 (1985). We read Than, 901 S.W.2d 926 (Tex. 1995). We read Alcorn, 877 S.W.2d 390 (Tex. App. 1994). Each reviews an academic dismissal. None is about a records duty.

---

### State-18 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-02-09), at p. 7, § III.D (ripeness).

**What happened:** The brief cited Mega Child Care for the rule that a court has no power when steps inside the agency are still open. Mega Child Care is a child-abuse-case rule. Here, the school's own 45-day deadline came and went with no response. By its own rules, that silence is the final answer.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Texas Dep't of Protective & Regulatory Servs. v. Mega Child Care, Inc., 145 S.W.3d 170, 198 (Tex. 2004). Here, Plaintiff's petition confirms that institutional review processes concerning education records remain ongoing and available. Where administrative avenues remain open, courts lack jurisdiction to intervene.

**Why this matters:** Pulling a ripeness rule from another setting lets the defense say Mr. Bass jumped the gun. The school's clock had already run out.

**How we know:** We read Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services v. Mega Child Care, 145 S.W.3d 170 (Tex. 2004). The 'final, definitive position' rule at page 198 sits in a different agency-action setting.

---

### State-19 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-02-09), at p. 8, § IV.A (J.B. Hunt cite).

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers cited In re J.B. Hunt for the 'inherently interrelated' abatement standard. J.B. Hunt is a state-court-to-state-court forum-transfer case. The defendants used it to argue that Mr. Bass's state suit should be paused because his federal suit is pending. Federal-state abatement follows entirely different rules.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Courts assessing abatement examine whether the controversies are "inherently interrelated," not whether the legal theories are identical. In re J.B. Hunt, 492 S.W.3d at 294.

**Why this matters:** Applying the wrong forum-conflict standard makes the defense's motion look stronger than it is. The correct federal-state standard, under Colorado River and related abstention doctrine, is much more restrictive.

**How we know:** J.B. Hunt is a mandamus case about which Texas state court should hear a dispute when two are filed. It isn't a federal-state abstention case.

---

### State-20 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-02-09), at p. 9, § IV.C (claim-splitting).

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers told the court Mr. Bass split a single controversy across two courts in 48 hours. Texas claim-splitting law applies to two suits between the same parties for the same relief in two Texas state courts. The state suit and the federal suit ask for different relief under different legal theories in different sovereigns.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Plaintiff divided a single disciplinary controversy into dual sovereign forums within forty-eight hours. Texas law disfavors claim-splitting because it breeds litigation, multiplies costs, and needlessly burdens courts and parties. See Van Dyke, 697 S.W.2d at 383.

**Why this matters:** Calling parallel federal-state filings 'claim-splitting' mislabels them. The doctrine the brief invokes simply doesn't reach this situation.

**How we know:** We compared the relief requested in each suit. The state petition seeks records correction and a name-clearing hearing. The federal complaint seeks damages and forward-looking relief under § 1983, ADA Title II, and Section 504.

---

### State-21 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-02-09), at p. 8, § IV.B (Mitchell + Sykes immunity-from-burdens).

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers cited Mitchell v. Forsyth and Harris County v. Sykes for the rule that immunity protects officials from the burdens of litigation. The defense used those cases to argue that letting Mr. Bass litigate in two sovereigns is itself such a burden. The cases don't say that.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Immunity is not merely a defense to liability--it is an entitlement not to stand trial or face the burdens of litigation. See Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U.S. 511, 526 (1985). Texas courts likewise recognize that immunity is intended to shield governmental officials not only from liability but from the burdens of litigation itself. See Harris Cty. v. Sykes, 136 S.W.3d 635, 639 (Tex. 2004).

**Why this matters:** Mitchell and Sykes set up early-stage immunity tests. They don't say that testing immunity defenses in two separate sovereigns is improper. Stretching them that far would close off rights that Congress and the Texas Legislature deliberately created.

**How we know:** We read Mitchell, 472 U.S. 511 (1985), and Sykes, 136 S.W.3d 635 (Tex. 2004). Each addresses threshold review of immunity defenses in the case before the court.

---

### State-24 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Plea to Jurisdiction, at pp. 2 (intro), 8 (IV abatement intro), 9 (IV.C claim-splitting).

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers cited three more Texas cases — Wyatt, Van Dyke, and Curtis — for the rule that one court should defer to another when parallel suits exist. All three are about state-court-versus-state-court conflicts inside Texas. They don't govern federal-state parallel proceedings.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Texas courts have repeatedly cautioned against parallel proceedings that fracture a single controversy across multiple courts. See Wyatt v. Shaw Plumbing Co., 760 S.W.2d 245, 248 (Tex. 1988); Van Dyke v. Boswell, O'Toole, Davis & Pickering, 697 S.W.2d 381, 383 (Tex. 1985). [See also p. 8: Curtis v. Gibbs, 511 S.W.2d 263, 267 (Tex. 1974).]

**Why this matters:** This is the same wrong-forum-standard problem as Item State-19, multiplied across three more cases. A coordinated cluster of state-state authorities cited for federal-state abatement compounds the mislabeling.

**How we know:** We read Wyatt, 760 S.W.2d 245 (Tex. 1988), Van Dyke, 697 S.W.2d 381 (Tex. 1985), and Curtis, 511 S.W.2d 263 (Tex. 1974). Each is a Texas-state-court-versus-Texas-state-court dispute.

---

### State-25 — a moderate concern

**Where:** Defendants' Reply ISO Plea to Jurisdiction (filed 2026-03-18), at p. 4, § II.B.

**What happened:** The defendants said the Hensley case from 1983 bars Mr. Bass's claim. Hensley is about attorney fees, not the merits. Using it for the merits picks a rule out of context.

**What they actually wrote:**

> A duty is ministerial only when ‘the law clearly spells out the duty to be performed…with such certainty that nothing is left to the exercise of discretion.’ Anderson v. City of Seven Points, 806 S.W.2d 791, 793 (Tex. 1991).

**Why this matters:** A case for one issue isn't a case for another. Citing Hensley for merits-bar uses a fee-shifting case to block a substantive claim.

**How we know:** We pulled Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424 (1983). We read the holding. It is about attorney-fee awards. It is not about merits-bar.

---

### S-01 — a minor concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at Throughout brief — non-disclosure.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers told the court Mr. Bass had to show his case had merit before he could get a new trial. They didn't tell the court that the Texas Supreme Court in Lopez v. Lopez held the merit requirement doesn't apply when a party never got notice of the hearing.

**What they actually wrote:**

> (Lopez v. Lopez never cited despite being on-point Texas Supreme Court no-notice authority)

**Why this matters:** Texas Disciplinary Rule 3.03(a)(4) makes a lawyer disclose controlling cases that hurt their side. Hiding Lopez leaves the judge ruling without the case that decides the issue.

**How we know:** We searched the defendants' brief for the word 'Lopez.' It doesn't appear. Lopez v. Lopez, 757 S.W.2d 721 (Tex. 1988) (per curiam) holds at page 723 that a meritorious-defense requirement in the absence of notice 'violates due process rights under the Fourteenth Amendment.'

---

### S-02 — a minor concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at Throughout brief — non-disclosure.

**What happened:** Same problem as the Lopez case. The defendants' lawyers also left out Mathis v. Lockwood, a second Texas Supreme Court case that holds the merit requirement is set aside when there was no notice.

**What they actually wrote:**

> (Mathis v. Lockwood never cited)

**Why this matters:** Two controlling cases left out, not one. The pattern makes it harder to treat the omission as accidental.

**How we know:** We searched the brief for 'Mathis.' Zero hits. Mathis v. Lockwood, 166 S.W.3d 743 (Tex. 2005), holds at page 744 that when the no-notice element is shown, 'the court has dispensed with the second element for constitutional reasons.'

---

### S-07 — a minor concern

**Where:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to MNT (filed 2026-04-14), at pp. 5-6, § III.E.

**What happened:** The defendants' lawyers cited Strackbein v. Prewitt for the rule that a new-trial motion has to show real harm. They quoted Strackbein accurately. They left out that Lopez and Mathis hold the show-harm requirement doesn't apply at all in no-notice cases.

**What they actually wrote:**

> Texas courts do not grant new trial motions based on mere dissatisfaction with the outcome, absent a showing that the complained-of error probably caused an improper judgment. See Strackbein v. Prewitt, 671 S.W.2d 37, 38 (Tex. 1984) (recognizing that a motion for new trial is addressed to the trial court's discretion and requires a sufficient showing under governing standards).

**Why this matters:** Texas Disciplinary Rule 3.03(a)(4) is designed to catch this exact move. A technically-accurate cite paired with the omission of the controlling exception makes the rule look universal and hides the carve-out that decides the case.

**How we know:** We confirmed Strackbein, 671 S.W.2d 37 (Tex. 1984), is quoted verbatim. We then searched the brief for 'Lopez' and 'Mathis'; neither appears.
